question: Is it permissible to economically boycott companies or countries that harm Muslims?
asked: What is the Islamic stance on economic boycotts: not purchasing goods from countries that have harmed Muslims, or from companies known for helping regimes or illegal occupation?
answer:
The response to this question is that this issue of economic boycott, it is an issue of tactics. It is an issue of means. It is an issue of methodology, not an issue of goals. And we need to understand that the Shari'ah has come with goals; it did not come with means. The Shari'ah came with a final, like, what do you need to do? And it did not tell you how to get to that need.

Let me give you a simple example. The Shari'ah told us to preach Islam to others. The Shari'ah did not tell us the specific methodology, the tactics of how to give da'wah. And therefore, for example, writing an op-ed in the newspaper: did the Sahaba ever write an op-ed in the newspaper? There were no newspapers to sway public opinion. Did they ever do that? In fact, even the concept of swaying public opinion in this type of manner: if you look at the letters of the Prophet ﷺ, it's a totally different time and place. He's inviting them straight to Islam. Excellent, beautiful. What if somebody were to do slightly different tactics? As I said, write an op-ed or article or whatnot in which we correct certain misinformation, without necessarily getting to the point of inviting them to Islam. That's a stepping stone; we're going to get there. Is there anything wrong with that?

The goal is da'wah. How specifically da'wah is done, using the internet, what we put on the internet, the methodology, the languages, the styles that we're going to use: all of this is from the tactics, and it is from the means to get to the goal. The goal is da'wah. The goal is inviting others to the way of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

Allah says in the Qur'an, "Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good preaching, and if you have to argue, argue in a manner that is the best with them." Now, all three of these are contextual. Call to your Lord with wisdom: anybody who is multicultural knows that wisdom, and how you say something, and the language that you use, and the tone that you use, and the examples that you give, and how strict or lenient you can be, it is culture-specific. Anybody who is multicultural knows this. How you would speak to somebody of this land would be different than how you speak to somebody from another land. It all goes back to your culture. So when Allah is saying, "Call to your Lord with wisdom," right then and there, wisdom varies from time and place and culture and society.

And Allah says good maw'idha. Maw'idha means emotional argument; maw'idha means you really get to their soul. Once again, this is something where the tactics and the methodology would vary from time to place to people. It's very specific, it's culture-specific. How I would speak to a Western audience, a non-Muslim audience, when I talk to them about Islam, is very different than, let's say, how somebody 500 years ago, in maybe another land, would speak to the people of that land. Very different. The examples I would give, the concepts I would bring up, the languages, everything would be totally different. And Allah is saying, call them with the best manner, and then, if you must argue, argue in the manner that is best as well. All three of these, Allah made culture-specific.

And the same goes when it comes to tactics that are meant to basically hurt those that are harming us. The same goes for, for example, the issue of economic boycotts. The goal is that anybody who harms us, we do not support them. That's the goal. Allah says in the Qur'an, "Cooperate in good and piety, and do not cooperate in evil, and do not cooperate in transgression." Now, there is a company that we know is harming people, harming Muslims; they're doing evil things. So boycotting them, if it is going to achieve a good goal, and if the experts tell us that there's going to be benefit in this, then definitely it is something that should be done. It becomes a tactic, because the goal, we all agree, is that we want to minimize harm. The goal is to minimize oppression, to hurt the oppressor so that they stop the oppression. So the tactics vary from time to place to situation.

And therefore, **economic boycotts are a tactic, and they are most definitely permissible.** They are ja'iz; it is permissible to do that. And in fact, the Quraysh themselves used this tactic against the Muslims. What was the boycott? You know the famous boycott, when the Prophet was in the Shi'b of the Banu Hashim, when the Muslims had to leave and live in the mountains for a while. What was that boycott? That boycott was that they would stop selling their goods to the Muslims, and stop intermarriage with the Muslims, and stop everything with the Muslims. So the Quraysh used economic boycott against Islam.

And a few years later, the Muslims of Medina, when they migrated, as well: there are references to them not engaging in general trade with the Quraysh, because they're not going to have peaceful trade anymore with the people that attempted to kill them. So they used that, and they in fact pinched the economic lifeline of the Quraysh multiple times. The Battle of Badr and Uhud and whatnot, that's one of the things that they were doing: they're pinching the lifeline. They began to make sure that that lifeline of the economic trade route became constricted, became difficult, and it can be seen as a tactic of economic boycott. Therefore, the notion of economic boycotts is something that we can actually derive from the Seerah itself, and there should be no problem in saying that it is completely permissible to engage in economic boycotts.

And these days, of course, the issue is coming about France in particular and what it is doing, and should we boycott French products and whatnot. And the answer to this is most definitely, if experts, if economic policy makers... because again, the point of boycotts: they have to be effective. They have to do something. And who is going to decide that? Not me. I'm not an economics expert, I'm not a political science expert. People who are in the business, people who know, they will tell us that, hey, if so many millions of Muslims stopped purchasing that product, it will be the most harmful to them. So we listen to the experts in the field, and the job of scholars is to listen to these experts and then propagate it to the people. And so therefore, definitely no problems in boycotts. No problem.

However, all of that having been said, two caveats. And please don't understand these caveats as being against the issue of boycotts. I've just told you, boycotts are a tactic that is halal and effective when it is done properly. That having been said, two caveats.

Firstly, we have to be accurate. We cannot be emotional. We have to understand the company or the country or whatnot: is it really sinful or evil, such that we should be boycotting it? And again, I don't want to be too specific, because I don't want to endorse a brand or whatnot, but let me just say there's a very popular coffee brand in America, one of the most popular brands, and there is this notion that this chain is a supporter of the apartheid regime of Israel: that if you purchase one coffee, you are literally... there's a meme going around that every coffee is like a bullet to our Palestinian brothers and sisters. I'm not endorsing the company (frankly, it has mediocre coffee, but that's beside the point). I'm not endorsing the company, I'm not criticizing, I'm just being factual here: that's just wrong. The company itself does not support any political entity. Yes, the founder, of his own personal wealth, might have a certain persuasion, and if you feel that, by the time you calculate what percentage goes to that person, you don't want to show up there, that's completely your prerogative. But in reality, boycotting that company is not going to save the life of any Muslim in the world, or harm the life of any Muslim. I'm sure you're going to save money; I'm not saying you're not going to. Each coffee is overpriced over there. You might save money; you can give it as sadaqah. But to make this an Islamic cause seems emotionalism.

The same goes for... again, when I was growing up in the 80s, we were taught that Pepsi stands for "Pay every penny to the state of Israel." I mean, these types of notions, they're just not true. I mean, I'm sure you should boycott Pepsi simply because of the sugar in it. No question about that. You should boycott it for health reasons; I'll be the number one on the list. But to claim that these companies, if you purchase them, you are killing Muslims or helping... Again, the problem comes that in the long run you're damaging your own... it's like the boy who cried wolf. You keep on saying everything is haram or related to this. It doesn't work that way. So be careful, and let the experts tell you. Don't just base your fatwas on memes on the internet and whatever people are passing around. Be a little bit more discerning in this regard.

The second, and this is the more technical, and perhaps some of you will not like what I'm saying, but I have to be clear in the eyes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Listen: **nobody can make it haram for you to purchase a product if Allah has not made it haram.** And people's circumstances are different. We can encourage, we can help people find alternatives, we can pass around legitimate information that these are the companies that should be boycotted. But at the end of the day, if a particular person, because of his or her circumstance, is not able to boycott, we should not shame that person if their circumstances force them to do that.

Let me give you a simple example: the French boycott. Now, obviously, all of us can easily boycott. I don't even know what the French produce. It's not as if they have a major economy; what is it for us? Cheese or some perfumes. I don't eat goat cheese anyway. It's not a major thing. But suppose everybody came together and boycotted French products. What do you expect French Muslims to do? They're going to boycott living in France? What do you expect them to do? They're living in the country. What's going to happen? Same goes: other countries might boycott the country we live in because of the war crimes and whatnot. You're paying your taxes; me and you are paying our taxes. So what are you going to tell them when they say, "We're not buying anything from that country," the country you live in, and you're paying taxes to that country? So there's two sides to the coin, always.

And feel free to boycott specific companies. No problem. Feel free to boycott countries even, and their products. No problem, and it's good. But don't make it Allah's wajib on other people. Don't bring in wajib and haram; don't use these terms. Say, let us collectively come together to put pressure. Excellent. Let us try our best to use the economic means. But do not make somebody sinful for something Allah has not made sinful.

During times when specific tribes of Medina, the Banu Qaynuqa', the Banu Qurayzah, the Banu Nadir, were causing problems for the Muslims, the Sahaba would still buy and sell, and there were business partnerships to the very end. To the very end there were business partnerships, because there was no alternative. They could not boycott those tribes. You could boycott the Quraysh, and they did boycott the Quraysh. They could not boycott those three tribes of the Bani Isra'il background, because they had the economic lifeline in Medina, and they controlled the market and resources. And the Muslims continued to buy and sell and to be business partners with these three tribes until each one of them... what happened to them happened. So we cannot make this a matter of 'aqidah, of theology, of haram and halal. The max we can say is: let's cooperate together, and let's try our best to put on pressure.

And also, again, let us be fair here, because again, there's a lot of emotionalism going on. It's very easy to boycott certain things, but to be consistent... people are going to call us out, right? To be consistent, you're going to be called out, because you cannot boycott each and everything that is harmful. Again, let's be very blunt here. There's a country here, let's call it by name, China. It is persecuting millions, millions of Muslims. Are you really going to boycott each and every product from China? Go through your house. I guarantee you 70%, 60% of your products are somehow related to that country. What are you going to do? Our hearts bleed for our Uyghur brothers and sisters. We make du'a for them. What is happening now is unprecedented since the times of World War II. Unprecedented: the largest concentration camps since the Nazis. And our hearts are in pain; we're making du'a for them. But that country is a superpower in terms of produce. To what level are you going to boycott? To what level?

The same goes for the apartheid regime. I boycott certain products from that regime. I boycott it. I do not buy anything that I know is using illegal settlements. I try my best and I make a point. But at the same time, there are products that are somehow linked to our companies as well, computer chips, this and that, that are produced in that country, and most of our computers have those products as well. So to what level are we going to boycott? I'm not saying that just because we cannot be fully consistent, we throw the baby out with the bathwater. I'm not saying that. But I'm asking us to be a little bit more mature and a little bit more realistic, and understand that there are times and places where economic boycott is possible and sensible, and then there are other times and places where it is neither possible nor sensible. So we leave it to the experts, and be in touch with those who understand the global economy and whatnot, and then see what we can do in this regard.

The Shari'ah itself allows it. It doesn't mandate it, and it doesn't make it sinful; the Shari'ah allows it. And my opinion, again, is that we allow the experts to speak. And therefore, given the current circumstances (right now, as we speak, there are major trials going on in France and whatnot against the Muslim community), I have no problem that we publicize that we're not going to purchase anything from France, and we have the luxury of doing that. Alhamdulillah, plenty of alternatives; no problem.

And the same goes, again, for me personally: I'm very, very conscious about anything that is made using land that has been confiscated, basically, from the settlements. Because again, the entire region is confiscated in its own way. It's an apartheid regime; they came in and they took the entire land, everything from the beginning. But there are certain lands that are even more illegal than other lands. And so any time there is a corporation that is operating in settlements, and you do your research, and we know exactly who they are, we should be extra careful, and we should publicize that we're not going to deal with any of them.

But if somebody goes and purchases them, are you going to say that Allah's la'n is on you, that it's haram? You cannot use that language. You cannot use that language, because with that language you are now infringing on the rights of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And Allah has not made it haram. Allah has made it a tactic, and whether you choose to use it or not, that's up to you.

And I personally, as I said, I expect Allah to reward me. I expect Allah to reward me when I do not purchase products made by Israeli companies that are operating in the illegal settlement areas. Literally, my kids: when I tell them, do not purchase this company, this company, we don't want any of these products, if one of them says it tastes better, I say, I don't care. One time I said, we're going to make it at home, no problem. I expect Allah to reward me, but at the same time, there must be a level of common sense and whatnot. And as I said, we don't bring haram and halal to other Muslims. You feel free to do it. You be as strict as you want. You encourage others to do it. In case somebody, for whatever reason, doesn't listen, that's their prerogative, and you don't know their circumstance, and you leave it to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.
